headline: Forest Collectors Finally Get Fair Pay Through Direct Sales
meta_description: An e-commerce platform is helping Indian forest collectors earn 28-35% higher prices by cutting out middlemen, transforming livelihoods across Jharkhand and be…
summary_short: A new online marketplace is connecting forest product collectors directly to buyers, helping them capture fair prices for mahua flowers, honey, and tendu leaves.
body:
For three years, Mamta Tigga from Gumla in Jharkhand has collected mahua flowers, air potato, and tendu leaves from the forest—work that keeps her family afloat when money runs short. Like most forest collectors, she saw almost none of the true value of her labor. A new review examining non-timber forest products across Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, and West Bengal's Sundarbans reveals the brutal mathematics: collectors receive less than 20 percent of what consumers ultimately pay, with tendu leaves showing a staggering sixfold price jump between collection and retail. But an e-commerce platform called e-TRIFED, run by India's Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation, is beginning to change this equation by linking producers directly with buyers and eliminating middlemen. Producer groups using the platform are already seeing 28 to 35 percent higher prices than those selling through conventional channels.

The work itself demands far more skill and knowledge than the word "collector" suggests. Harvesting honey from wild giant honeybee colonies in the Sundarbans, for instance, requires specialized techniques passed down through generations—harvesters use smoke to pacify the bees in dangerous nighttime operations. Yet urban markets rarely see this expertise. Women account for 60 to 80 percent of India's forest product collection workforce but have historically captured only a fraction of market revenues.

Researchers argue that integrating traditional ecological knowledge—such as collecting mahua flowers only after they naturally fall, or rotating harvest areas to allow regeneration—with formal forest management could help communities adapt as climate change disrupts rainfall patterns and flowering cycles. When blockchain systems can trace exactly who was paid what for each jar of honey or bundle of leaves, consumers gain transparency and collectors gain dignity. The platform represents a quiet revolution: rural communities no longer treated as footnotes to the forest economy, but recognized as the skilled entrepreneurs they have always been.
quick_facts: Collectors capture less than 20% of final consumer price for forest products
Tendu leaves show sixfold price multiplication from collection to retail
e-TRIFED users earn 28-35% higher prices than conventional intermediaries
Women comprise 60-80% of India's forest product collection workforce
Mahua flowers, honey, and tendu leaves sustain millions in Jharkhand and West Bengal
